newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto's ouster gives shaken Pakistan fresh start.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto's ouster gives shaken Pakistan fresh start.

text.p: President Farooq Leghari's abrupt dismissal of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto sent tremors of uncertainty mixed with hope through Pakistan on Tuesday.
Bhutto was sacked for a second time in her turbulent political career, by different presidents. Both times her government was accused of corruption, nepotism and misrule.
The head of state struck down Bhutto's three-year-old administration and dissolved parliament in the early hours as army troops moved into Islamabad to take over key installations.
Some popular jubilation, but no violence, was reported in what appears to have been a planned action that had army support and was within the president's constitutional powers.
The military kept a low profile. But political observers said the president could not have acted without the approval and cooperation of the generals.
Leghari's dismissal of Bhutto, once a political ally, was another jolt in the fragile democratic life of a nation that has been under military rule for 24 years of its 49-year history.
The outside world was looking to Pakistan's new interim prime minister, Meraj Khalid, 80, to steer the country to new elections on February 3, the date set by Leghari.
Visiting British shadow foreign secretary Robin Cook said serious problems, including economic chaos and rows over the judiciary and corruption, had marred Bhutto's administration.

"Obviously the interest of the international community is that the election commitment be honoured and that the agreement with the IMF (International Monetary Fund) be maintained," he told Reuters by telephone.
It was not clear what lay in store for Bhutto, who could not be reached at her official residence after her removal, or for her husband Asif Ali Zardari, detained by troops in Lahore.
Bhutto, 43, had defended Zardari, named investment minister in July, from opposition charges of corruption, but her denials failed to purify his tarnished public reputation.
Leghari, whose own name for honesty has survived corruption allegations, kept public silence in the hours after his dramatic move to oust Bhutto, as rumours flew about his intentions.
Uncertainty blended with relief that Bhutto's downfall had been achieved without bloodshed. Investors crowded to the Karachi Stock Exchange even though it was closed for a holiday.

Share prices jumped in kerb trading in the bourse's parking lot and dealer Salman Ahmed said investors seemed pleased. "They hope the new caretaker set-up will take care of corruption, mismanagement and the law and order situation," he said.

Bhutto had been plagued by successive crises, including ethnic unrest in Karachi, sectarian violence between Shi'ite and Sunni Moslems and economic woes that trapped Pakistan in an stop-go relationship with the IMF.
Scoffing at her critics and warning darkly of unnamed conspirators against her ill-starred family, she had sworn to keep going until scheduled elections in October 1998.

Internationally she strove to paint herself as a moderate leader of an Islamic nation of 131 million people, fending off threats from Moslem radicals at home and arguing Pakistan's case against arch-rival India in the long-running Kashmir dispute.
But she suffered a devastating personal blow in September when police in Karachi shot dead her estranged brother Murtaza Bhutto for reasons that have yet to be adequately explained.

Bhutto is no stranger to tragedy. Her other brother, Shahnawaz, died, apparently of poisoning in France in 1985, and her father, former prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, was hanged in 1979 on a disputed conviction for conspiring to commit a political murder.
Leghari accused Bhutto's government of fostering corruption, undermining the judiciary and failing to stop extra-judicial killings in Karachi and elsewhere.
A European diplomat questioned why Leghari, if he had information about summary killings, did not speak out before.

"Corruption, nepotism and violation of rules in the administration of the affairs of the government... has become so extensive and widespread that the orderly functioning of government in accordance of the provisions of the constitution and the law has become impossible and in some cases, national security has been endangered," Leghari said in a proclamation.
"Public faith in the integrity and honesty of the government has disappeared," he added.
Bhutto had been in power since general elections in October 1993. Her first term lasted 20 months before then president Ghulam Ishaq Khan sacked her in 1990 for alleged corruption.
The president has constitutional powers to dismiss elected governments and dissolve parliament's lower house.
